newsitem.title: UK: World oil prices edge up on Nigerian export worries.
newsitem.headline: World oil prices edge up on Nigerian export worries.

text.p: Oil markets edged nervously higher on Thursday amid uncertainty about possible cuts to Nigerian oil exports.
Many oil traders remain bearish but even a hint of lower exports ahead of the Easter holiday period was enough to trigger a small wave of short-covering.

London's May futures for North Sea bellwether Brent Blend crude were up 12 cents at $19.41 a barrel at 1700 GMT. Prices for Brent have fallen from just under $25 a barrel to what many dealers see as a temporary low of less than $19 at the start of this month.

"Unless any export cut is extended it won't have a big impact on the market. But even a small chance is enough to provoke some defensive short-covering," said Scott Carter, senior oil trader at Tosco Petroleum UK in London.

Spreading communal unrest in Nigeria, Africa's biggest oil producer, has cut daily crude output by 10 percent this week and threatens imminent disruption to exports, state and foreign oil companies warned on Thursday.

Six installations in the oil-rich Niger Delta, operated by the Anglo-Dutch giant Royal Dutch/Shell were overrun last Saturday by villagers involved in local government disputes and were still occupied on Thursday. Five more were shut in response to demands from community groups but were not occupied.

Shell, which produces about half the country's daily output of 2.15 million barrels, and state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC) said exports would be disrupted if the disturbances did not end soon.

"There are no cancellations yet, but if things continue beyond where they are today there will be cancellations," an NNPC official said. Nigeria depends on crude exports for more than 90 percent of its foreign exchange earnings.
Shell warned customers on Wednesday it may be forced to cancel or delay exports early next month unless it could restore the 210,000 barrels per day (bpd) of production lost since Saturday.
"If we are talking about a possible force majeure from April 2, then clearly we need to resume production quickly to avoid that," a Shell official told Reuters.
Meanwhile, the crude oil market in the Atlantic remains awash with crude and only a pick-up in gasoline demand from the United States is likely to rescue world prices, say traders.
Most oil products were buckling under pressure of oversupply as refiners, some resuming after maintenance shutdowns, kept running close to flat out.
Gasoline was lower and heating oil in Europe was also taking a beating, traders said.
